## Summary

We are a global, faith-based nonprofit that works with local communities around the world to develop language solutions that expand possibilities for a better life. SIL's core contribution areas are Bible translation, literacy, education, development, linguistic research and language tools.   
  
 We are eager for the day when all people enjoy equal access to education, to socio-economic opportunities, and to resources for spiritual growth - no matter what language they speak or sign.

## Purpose

We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most.   
  
 SIL's service with ethnolinguistic minority communities is motivated by the belief that all people are created in the image of God, and that languages and cultures are part of the richness of God's creation. SIL is founded on the principle that communities should be able to pursue their social, cultural, political, economic and spiritual goals without sacrificing their ethnolinguistic identity. As a faith-based nonprofit organization, SIL works alongside language communities as they discover how to harness the power of their language to address challenges and reach their goals.

* * *

## Mission statement

Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture.

## History

The principal founder of SIL International was William Cameron Townsend (1896-1982). He began cross-cultural work with the Kaqchikel people of Guatemala in 1919. By 1929, Townsend's vision had broadened to include other peoples who also needed language development. SIL International (then known as the Summer Institute of Linguistics) began in 1934 as a summer training program in Arkansas, USA, with two students. The enrollment of these summer classes grew each subsequent year.   
  
 Kenneth L. Pike (1912-2000) was one of five students in the 1935 course. He began work on the Mixtec language in the state of Oaxaca, Mexico. This work launched Pike into his life-long work in linguistics and the study of language in the context of human behavior. Dr. Pike served as President of SIL until 1979.   
  
 For a timeline, visit: sil.org/about/history

* * *

## Program accomplishments

As of October 2021, we are involved in approximately 1,633 active language projects in 98 countries. These projects impact more than 855+ million people within 1,347 local communities. SIL's work brings together more than 4,200 staff from 84 countries who work alongside thousands more local partners and community volunteers worldwide.

## Purpose

 SIL's service with ethnolinguistic minority communities is motivated by the belief that all people are created in the image of God, and that languages and cultures are part of the richness of God's creation. SIL is founded on the principle that communities should be able to pursue their social, cultural, political, economic and spiritual goals without sacrificing their ethnolinguistic identity. # About SIL Global

### [![Image 2](https://www.sila.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/sil_glyph_logo_taiheritagepro_rgb500px-300x161.png.webp)](https://www.sil.org/)

[SIL Global](https://www.sil.org/)is a global, faith-based nonprofit that works with local communities around the world to develop language solutions that expand possibilities for a better life.

#### Faith & Service

Our faith inspires and informs our commitment to expand possibilities for people to thrive. We believe all people are created by God and given language as a means for flourishing. Through language, we understand who we are, experience relationships and explore life’s most important questions.

As followers of Jesus, we believe:

*   **All people are important.**That’s why we care about all languages.
*   **Relationship with God is precious.**That’s why we pray, love the Bible and support its translation so others can have the same opportunities to know God better.
*   **All aspects of a person’s life matter.**That’s why we work toward language solutions that advance learning, health, justice, reconciliation and spiritual growth.

#### Language Development

SIL works with ethnolinguistic minority communities as they build their capacity for the sustainable development of their own languages.

*   Community-based language development involves a series of ongoing planned actions that a language community takes to ensure that its language continues to serve its changing social, cultural, political, economic and spiritual needs and goals. SIL’s expertise related to language development includes training and consulting for activities such as linguistic analysis, orthography and writing systems development, literature development, multilingual education and literacy.

#### Materials Development

SIL works in partnership with local speakers to develop new written and oral materials in their mother tongue.

*   The format of mother-tongue materials is determined by the community and might include print, audio or video items. Content covers a variety of subjects such as primers, folk stories, schoolbooks, health and hygiene guidelines, games, history, etc. In addition to original publications, local translators often adapt educational materials from other languages on subjects such as nutrition, farming and health (including HIV/AIDS). SIL also works with communities to foster the effective use of these resources.

#### Academic Research

Over 950 of SIL’s workers hold advanced degrees, and many regularly present papers and publish their research.

*   Through extensive language survey efforts, SIL is a leader in the identification and documentation of the world’s languages. Results of this research are published in [Ethnologue: Languages of the World](https://www.ethnologue.com/), a comprehensive catalogue of the world’s 7,000+ living languages.  
 SIL has over 60,000 resources in its Language and Culture Archives and is adding an average of 1,700 new items annually. Online, SIL provides citations for 38,200 of these resources and approximately 4,100 of these resources are available for download. The other resources cited may be available upon request through [SIL Global Publications](https://www.sil.org/resources/publications).

#### Training

SIL offers training in a variety of disciplines relevant to sustainable language development.

*   SIL offers training in fields of study that support language development such as linguistics, literacy and multilingual education, anthropology, translation and learner-directed language and culture learning. SIL training is available for members of minority language communities, for policymakers and educators concerned with minority language issues, and for those who wish to assist communities in their language development efforts.  
 Training is available in numerous formats, from short courses and workshops to full degree programs offered in cooperation with universities and educational institutions worldwide.

#### Partnerships

SIL’s primary partnerships are with local language communities and with other agencies serving them.

*   In many locations, SIL has agreements to provide expertise, training or consulting for language development with universities, government departments or local organisations involved in education, development or Christian service.  
 SIL has been an official NGO partner with UNESCO since 1993 and has had special consultative status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) since 1997. SIL is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.  
 SIL also partners with other faith-based organizations that are committed to the social and justice needs of minority peoples. SIL is a member of the Micah Network and the Forum of Bible Agencies International. Primary partners for funding and volunteer staff are organizations affiliated with Wycliffe Global Alliance.

#### Technology for Language Development

Technology brings much of the world together, yet can also be a barrier to participation of some communities in the global community.

*   SIL software supports fieldwork in linguistics and anthropology by streamlining collection, analysis and archiving of language and culture data. SIL facilitates the development of fonts for non-Roman and complex scripts so that language communities and people working with them are able to use their writing systems with technology such as computers and mobile devices.  
 A project of SIL Global’s Non-Roman Script Initiative, ScriptSource, provides valuable information about the world’s scripts and alphabets. It currently provides access to information on over 170 scripts used for the writing systems of thousands of languages.

#### Translation

SIL is involved in translation work in partnership with more than one thousand language communities around the world.

*   SIL provides training and technical support for community-based translation of materials such as books and booklets for educational programs, stories related to culture and folklore, health and community development resources and scripture texts. SIL facilitates the translation of scripture in contexts where such activity is within the scope of local working agreements and where translation of scripture texts has been identified by the community as a desired resource for spiritual development. The translation goals for each language are decided in close interaction with communities and partner agencies.  
 Translation in SIL focuses on:
    *   research and development in translation theory and practice
    *   academic training programs related to translation
    *   consultant and technical support for producing quality translations of texts
    *   building capacity within ethnolinguistic minority communities for translation of materials of particular interest to them

#### Advocacy

A history of engaging with communities in language development has given SIL insight into policies and structures that support local efforts.

*   SIL serves as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities, assisting them in raising awareness of their needs to governments, organisations and individuals whose policies and practices can promote and facilitate language development. Through language research, documentation and promotion of language development, SIL contributes to the preservation of languages and cultures in danger of disappearing.

# About SIL Global

### [![Image 2](https://www.sila.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/sil_glyph_logo_taiheritagepro_rgb500px-300x161.png.webp)](https://www.sil.org/)

[SIL Global](https://www.sil.org/)is a global, faith-based nonprofit that works with local communities around the world to develop language solutions that expand possibilities for a better life.

#### Faith & Service

Our faith inspires and informs our commitment to expand possibilities for people to thrive. We believe all people are created by God and given language as a means for flourishing. Through language, we understand who we are, experience relationships and explore life’s most important questions.

As followers of Jesus, we believe:

*   **All people are important.**That’s why we care about all languages.
*   **Relationship with God is precious.**That’s why we pray, love the Bible and support its translation so others can have the same opportunities to know God better.
*   **All aspects of a person’s life matter.**That’s why we work toward language solutions that advance learning, health, justice, reconciliation and spiritual growth.

#### Language Development

SIL works with ethnolinguistic minority communities as they build their capacity for the sustainable development of their own languages.

*   Community-based language development involves a series of ongoing planned actions that a language community takes to ensure that its language continues to serve its changing social, cultural, political, economic and spiritual needs and goals. SIL’s expertise related to language development includes training and consulting for activities such as linguistic analysis, orthography and writing systems development, literature development, multilingual education and literacy.

#### Materials Development

SIL works in partnership with local speakers to develop new written and oral materials in their mother tongue.

*   The format of mother-tongue materials is determined by the community and might include print, audio or video items. Content covers a variety of subjects such as primers, folk stories, schoolbooks, health and hygiene guidelines, games, history, etc. In addition to original publications, local translators often adapt educational materials from other languages on subjects such as nutrition, farming and health (including HIV/AIDS). SIL also works with communities to foster the effective use of these resources.

#### Academic Research

Over 950 of SIL’s workers hold advanced degrees, and many regularly present papers and publish their research.

*   Through extensive language survey efforts, SIL is a leader in the identification and documentation of the world’s languages. Results of this research are published in [Ethnologue: Languages of the World](https://www.ethnologue.com/), a comprehensive catalogue of the world’s 7,000+ living languages.  
 SIL has over 60,000 resources in its Language and Culture Archives and is adding an average of 1,700 new items annually. Online, SIL provides citations for 38,200 of these resources and approximately 4,100 of these resources are available for download. The other resources cited may be available upon request through [SIL Global Publications](https://www.sil.org/resources/publications).

#### Training

SIL offers training in a variety of disciplines relevant to sustainable language development.

*   SIL offers training in fields of study that support language development such as linguistics, literacy and multilingual education, anthropology, translation and learner-directed language and culture learning. SIL training is available for members of minority language communities, for policymakers and educators concerned with minority language issues, and for those who wish to assist communities in their language development efforts.  
 Training is available in numerous formats, from short courses and workshops to full degree programs offered in cooperation with universities and educational institutions worldwide.

#### Partnerships

SIL’s primary partnerships are with local language communities and with other agencies serving them.

*   In many locations, SIL has agreements to provide expertise, training or consulting for language development with universities, government departments or local organisations involved in education, development or Christian service.  
 SIL has been an official NGO partner with UNESCO since 1993 and has had special consultative status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) since 1997. SIL is a founding member of Maaya, the World Network for Linguistic Diversity.  
 SIL also partners with other faith-based organizations that are committed to the social and justice needs of minority peoples. SIL is a member of the Micah Network and the Forum of Bible Agencies International. Primary partners for funding and volunteer staff are organizations affiliated with Wycliffe Global Alliance.

#### Technology for Language Development

Technology brings much of the world together, yet can also be a barrier to participation of some communities in the global community.

*   SIL software supports fieldwork in linguistics and anthropology by streamlining collection, analysis and archiving of language and culture data. SIL facilitates the development of fonts for non-Roman and complex scripts so that language communities and people working with them are able to use their writing systems with technology such as computers and mobile devices.  
 A project of SIL Global’s Non-Roman Script Initiative, ScriptSource, provides valuable information about the world’s scripts and alphabets. It currently provides access to information on over 170 scripts used for the writing systems of thousands of languages.

#### Translation

SIL is involved in translation work in partnership with more than one thousand language communities around the world.

*   SIL provides training and technical support for community-based translation of materials such as books and booklets for educational programs, stories related to culture and folklore, health and community development resources and scripture texts. SIL facilitates the translation of scripture in contexts where such activity is within the scope of local working agreements and where translation of scripture texts has been identified by the community as a desired resource for spiritual development. The translation goals for each language are decided in close interaction with communities and partner agencies.  
 Translation in SIL focuses on:
    *   research and development in translation theory and practice
    *   academic training programs related to translation
    *   consultant and technical support for producing quality translations of texts
    *   building capacity within ethnolinguistic minority communities for translation of materials of particular interest to them

#### Advocacy

A history of engaging with communities in language development has given SIL insight into policies and structures that support local efforts.

*   SIL serves as an advocate for ethnolinguistic communities, assisting them in raising awareness of their needs to governments, organisations and individuals whose policies and practices can promote and facilitate language development. Through language research, documentation and promotion of language development, SIL contributes to the preservation of languages and cultures in danger of disappearing.

 Endangered Languages, Language Revitalization, Linguistic Diversity, Community-Based Strategies, Education Policy, Digital Technology, Cultural Heritage 
## Abstract

Endangered languages are among the most critical challenges in preserving human cultural and intellectual diversity. More than 40% of the world’s 7,000 languages are currently at risk of extinction. This narrative review examines global strategies for language revitalization, focusing on the roles of communities, education, technology, policy, and cultural identity. Literature was gathered from major academic databases (Scopus, PubMed, Google Scholar) using core keywords such as _language revitalization_ and _endangered languages_. The findings show that community-based initiatives, such as language nests and cultural integration, are crucial for intergenerational transmission. Education policies that include minority languages in school curricula foster measurable gains, while the absence of institutional support often results in stagnation. Digital tools expand access and engagement, though their effectiveness depends on cultural adaptation and community participation. Government recognition and funding further determine success, with marked disparities between developed and developing regions. Overall, language revitalization is not only a linguistic concern but also a matter of identity, cultural resilience, and social justice.

# Community, Education, and Technology in Language Revitalization: A Narrative Review

## Authors

*    Rajkamal D  St. Thomas College of Arts and Science 
*    Arik Susanti  Universitas Negeri Surabaya 

## DOI:

[https://doi.org/10.61978/lingua.v3i2.1039](https://doi.org/10.61978/lingua.v3i2.1039)
## Keywords:

 Endangered Languages, Language Revitalization, Linguistic Diversity, Community-Based Strategies, Education Policy, Digital Technology, Cultural Heritage 
## Abstract

Endangered languages are among the most critical challenges in preserving human cultural and intellectual diversity. More than 40% of the world’s 7,000 languages are currently at risk of extinction. This narrative review examines global strategies for language revitalization, focusing on the roles of communities, education, technology, policy, and cultural identity. Literature was gathered from major academic databases (Scopus, PubMed, Google Scholar) using core keywords such as _language revitalization_ and _endangered languages_. The findings show that community-based initiatives, such as language nests and cultural integration, are crucial for intergenerational transmission. Education policies that include minority languages in school curricula foster measurable gains, while the absence of institutional support often results in stagnation. Digital tools expand access and engagement, though their effectiveness depends on cultural adaptation and community participation. Government recognition and funding further determine success, with marked disparities between developed and developing regions. Overall, language revitalization is not only a linguistic concern but also a matter of identity, cultural resilience, and social justice.

# About Us

![Image 7](https://www.silglobal.site/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/481819738_1028106992678530_3781395677498780286_n-e1755637541957.jpg)

##### Serving the world’s language communities since 1934.

#### SIL Global is a community of local organizations that partner with minority language communities to help them use their languages to know God, learn freely, and live with dignity.

Many people around the world face hardship and discrimination because of the languages they speak or sign. We walk alongside 1,572 language communities in 119 countries to help turn those barriers of exclusion into bridges for flourishing.

## Our Vision & Mission

#### **A century-long calling, still alive today.**

###### VISION

We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most.

###### MISSION

Inspired by God’s love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture.

## Our Why

Our faith inspires and informs our commitment to expand possibilities for people to thrive. We believe all people are created by God and given language as a means for flourishing. Through language, we understand who we are, experience relationships and explore life’s most important questions.

As followers of Jesus, we believe:

*   All people are important.That’s why we care about all languages.
*   Relationship with God is precious.That’s why we pray, love the Bible and support its translation so others can have the same opportunities to know God better.
*   All aspects of a person’s life matter.That’s why we work toward language solutions that advance learning, health, justice, reconciliation and spiritual growth.

![Image 8](https://www.silglobal.site/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/481232950_1032266018929294_3404061641417964311_n-e1750717038592.jpg)

## Our Leadership

*   ![Image 9](https://global.sil.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/Johnstone-Ndunde-1920x1920.jpg)### Meet Our  
Executive Director 
**Dr. Johnstone Ndunde** became SIL Global’s Executive Director in May 2025, bringing 20 years of leadership in Bible translation, literacy, and language development across Africa, with a strong focus on collaboration, education, and flourishing language communities.

Learn More   ![Image 10](https://global.sil.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/Johnstone-Ndunde-1920x1920.jpg) #### Dr. Johnstone Ndunde Executive Director [This link is hidden to users via Advanced>Conditional Display and a trick to get the cursor at the top of the popup instead of the button at the bottom](https://global.silglobal.site/a-leadership-transition-conversation/) Dr. Johnstone Ndunde became SIL Global’s Executive Director in May 2025. He brings 20 years of experience in leadership, Bible translation, literacy, and language development across Africa, having served with SIL Global and before that Bible Translation and Literacy (BTL) in Kenya. His work has been rooted in advancing educational and spiritual opportunities within African language communities so individuals and communities can flourish In previous roles, Dr. Ndunde guided programs developing initiatives and instructional materials in schools and adult education in a number of countries in Africa. As Director of Strategy and then Area Director for SIL Anglo-Lusophone Africa, he fostered collaboration with key partners and church communities, expanded regional and global funding capabilities, and implemented initiatives to develop emerging leaders. Dr. Ndunde holds a Ph.D. in Leadership and Governance from Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, an MA in Educational Studies from Africa International University, and a B.Ed. in Commerce and Economics from the University of Nairobi. Fluent in English and Kiswahili, and a native speaker of Lunyole and a number of Luhyia languages, he brings valuable cultural insight and linguistic skills to his work. Dr. Ndunde lives in Nairobi, Kenya, with his wife, Esther. [Learn more about Dr. Ndunde](https://global.sil.org/a-leadership-transition-conversation/)           

###### Meet More Leaders

See the profiles of our leadership staff.

[View all leaders](https://global.sil.org/our-leaders)

## Our History

#### People & Language. For over 90 years.

In 1917, a young American named Cameron Townsend traveled through Guatemala selling Spanish Bibles. He soon realized that the indigenous people couldn’t use his Bibles – they didn’t speak Spanish. He also saw that they were oppressed in ways that affected all parts of their lives: their faith, language, social standing, and economic health.

Townsend founded the Summer Institute of Linguistics in 1934 as a summer training program for linguists to work with local people like those in Guatemala. Today we are SIL Global, a multicultural community of local organizations working, with over 1,500 language communities throughout the world.

![Image 11](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1930s.png)

##### 1930s

Cameron Townsend founded the Summer Institute of Linguistics to serve language communities on the margins of society.

More and more students came to study linguistics and went on to work in Mexico.

##### 1940s

SIL began work in North America among the Navajo and in South America in Peru.

![Image 12](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1940s.png)

![Image 13](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1950s.png)

##### 1950s

The first edition of Ethnologue described 46 languages. This comprehensive catalogue of the world’s living languages now describes over 7,000 languages.

SIL began work in the Pacific (Papua New Guinea) and Asia (the Philippines).

##### 1960s

SIL initiated work in Africa, partnering with communities in Ghana, Cameroon and Nigeria.

The Chuj New Testament in Guatemala was the first to be typeset by computer.

![Image 14](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1960s.png)

![Image 15](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1970s.png)

##### 1970s

SIL linguists began using portable computers, harnessing digital power for language work.

##### 1980s

Shell Books were created to help communities create their own books.

CARLA, a program that uses related languages to create drafts, was first used in Eastern Kakchiquel in Guatemala.

![Image 16](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1980s.png)

![Image 17](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1990s.png)

##### 1990s

SIL was granted UNESCO Consultative Status + ECOSOC Consultative Status.

Trauma Healing programs began in response to the Rwandan genocide. As of 2025, the materials are available in 175 languages. ([THI site](https://traumahealinginstitute.org/about)).

##### 2000s

SIL began using computers to design fonts for languages with complex scripts.

Sign language work began. With around 150 sign languages formally identified so far, researchers estimate that the actual number may exceed 400.

![Image 18](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2000s.png)

# About Us

![Image 7](https://www.silglobal.site/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/481819738_1028106992678530_3781395677498780286_n-e1755637541957.jpg)

##### Serving the world’s language communities since 1934.

#### SIL Global is a community of local organizations that partner with minority language communities to help them use their languages to know God, learn freely, and live with dignity.

Many people around the world face hardship and discrimination because of the languages they speak or sign. We walk alongside 1,572 language communities in 119 countries to help turn those barriers of exclusion into bridges for flourishing.

## Our Vision & Mission

#### **A century-long calling, still alive today.**

###### VISION

We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most.

###### MISSION

Inspired by God’s love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture.

## Our Why

Our faith inspires and informs our commitment to expand possibilities for people to thrive. We believe all people are created by God and given language as a means for flourishing. Through language, we understand who we are, experience relationships and explore life’s most important questions.

As followers of Jesus, we believe:

*   All people are important.That’s why we care about all languages.
*   Relationship with God is precious.That’s why we pray, love the Bible and support its translation so others can have the same opportunities to know God better.
*   All aspects of a person’s life matter.That’s why we work toward language solutions that advance learning, health, justice, reconciliation and spiritual growth.

![Image 8](https://www.silglobal.site/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/481232950_1032266018929294_3404061641417964311_n-e1750717038592.jpg)

## Our Leadership

*   ![Image 9](https://global.sil.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/Johnstone-Ndunde-1920x1920.jpg)### Meet Our  
Executive Director 
**Dr. Johnstone Ndunde** became SIL Global’s Executive Director in May 2025, bringing 20 years of leadership in Bible translation, literacy, and language development across Africa, with a strong focus on collaboration, education, and flourishing language communities.

Learn More   ![Image 10](https://global.sil.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/Johnstone-Ndunde-1920x1920.jpg) #### Dr. Johnstone Ndunde Executive Director [This link is hidden to users via Advanced>Conditional Display and a trick to get the cursor at the top of the popup instead of the button at the bottom](https://global.silglobal.site/a-leadership-transition-conversation/) Dr. Johnstone Ndunde became SIL Global’s Executive Director in May 2025. He brings 20 years of experience in leadership, Bible translation, literacy, and language development across Africa, having served with SIL Global and before that Bible Translation and Literacy (BTL) in Kenya. His work has been rooted in advancing educational and spiritual opportunities within African language communities so individuals and communities can flourish In previous roles, Dr. Ndunde guided programs developing initiatives and instructional materials in schools and adult education in a number of countries in Africa. As Director of Strategy and then Area Director for SIL Anglo-Lusophone Africa, he fostered collaboration with key partners and church communities, expanded regional and global funding capabilities, and implemented initiatives to develop emerging leaders. Dr. Ndunde holds a Ph.D. in Leadership and Governance from Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, an MA in Educational Studies from Africa International University, and a B.Ed. in Commerce and Economics from the University of Nairobi. Fluent in English and Kiswahili, and a native speaker of Lunyole and a number of Luhyia languages, he brings valuable cultural insight and linguistic skills to his work. Dr. Ndunde lives in Nairobi, Kenya, with his wife, Esther. [Learn more about Dr. Ndunde](https://global.sil.org/a-leadership-transition-conversation/)

## Our History

#### People & Language. For over 90 years.

In 1917, a young American named Cameron Townsend traveled through Guatemala selling Spanish Bibles. He soon realized that the indigenous people couldn’t use his Bibles – they didn’t speak Spanish. He also saw that they were oppressed in ways that affected all parts of their lives: their faith, language, social standing, and economic health.

Townsend founded the Summer Institute of Linguistics in 1934 as a summer training program for linguists to work with local people like those in Guatemala. Today we are SIL Global, a multicultural community of local organizations working, with over 1,500 language communities throughout the world.

![Image 11](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1930s.png)

##### 1930s

Cameron Townsend founded the Summer Institute of Linguistics to serve language communities on the margins of society.

More and more students came to study linguistics and went on to work in Mexico.

##### 1940s

SIL began work in North America among the Navajo and in South America in Peru.

![Image 12](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1940s.png)

![Image 13](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1950s.png)

##### 1950s

The first edition of Ethnologue described 46 languages. This comprehensive catalogue of the world’s living languages now describes over 7,000 languages.

SIL began work in the Pacific (Papua New Guinea) and Asia (the Philippines).

##### 1960s

SIL initiated work in Africa, partnering with communities in Ghana, Cameroon and Nigeria.

The Chuj New Testament in Guatemala was the first to be typeset by computer.

![Image 14](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1960s.png)

![Image 15](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1970s.png)

##### 1970s

SIL linguists began using portable computers, harnessing digital power for language work.

##### 1980s

Shell Books were created to help communities create their own books.

CARLA, a program that uses related languages to create drafts, was first used in Eastern Kakchiquel in Guatemala.

![Image 16](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1980s.png)

![Image 17](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/1990s.png)

##### 1990s

SIL was granted UNESCO Consultative Status + ECOSOC Consultative Status.

Trauma Healing programs began in response to the Rwandan genocide. As of 2025, the materials are available in 175 languages. ([THI site](https://traumahealinginstitute.org/about)).

##### 2000s

SIL began using computers to design fonts for languages with complex scripts.

Sign language work began. With around 150 sign languages formally identified so far, researchers estimate that the actual number may exceed 400.

![Image 18](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2000s.png)

![Image 19](https://silorgstg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2010s-1.png)

##### 2010s

Dr. Michel Kenmogne became SIL’s first non-western executive director.

Bloom book-making software was launched, enabling creation of books in any language with any script.

The 1000th New Testament with SIL involvement was published.

##### 2020s

SIL became a global community of locally-rooted organizations.

Dr. Johnstone Ndunde became SIL’s 9th executive director.

# Thriving Communities

![Image 6](https://www.silglobal.site/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2018Aug_Uganda_020.jpg)

#### Many language communities lack access to vital information for health, work, and family life in a language they understand.

This exclusion weakens communities over time and limits people’s ability to make informed decisions, participate in society, or sustain their communities. Communities may feel pressure to abandon their own language to survive — losing part of their identity, dignity, and belonging in the process.

## Our Approach

SIL helps language communities use their own languages to strengthen individual and community wellbeing. We walk alongside local leaders and organizations to develop tools, programs, and communication resources that meet real needs — from trauma healing and health education to sustainable livelihoods and language revitalization.

Language is foundational to community life, shaping how people make meaning together, transmit values, resolve conflict, and participate in society. When communities can access life-changing knowledge and express themselves in the language of the heart, they are better equipped to strengthen relationships, care for one another, and live with confidence and dignity.

**When communities use their own languages to address the realities of daily life, they can:**

*    Heal from trauma and rebuild trust and social bonds. 
*    Discuss sensitive topics in culturally meaningful and constructive ways. 
*    Prevent and treat illness more effectively through clear, trusted information. 
*    Strengthen families, churches and communities through faith and mutual care. 
*    Participate fully in society without giving up a part of who they are. 
*    Live with dignity, knowing their language and culture have value in the wider world. 

## Featured Story

###### “When My Own Healing Began”

Abraham Gahano, a pastor from a conflict-torn area in southern Ethiopia, knows pain. During one violent outbreak, he even watched his home be burned to the ground. As a pastor, he felt responsible to remain strong for his people, yet at times the pain inside seemed impossible to carry.

Everything changed when Abraham attended a trauma healing workshop conducted in his own language. In that space, surrounded by others who shared his experiences, something shifted.

**“I had never allowed myself to cry before,” he said. “But there, I felt safe. I shared my grief, and I wept. We wept together. And I truly understood that I am not alone. That moment of release — that is when my own healing began.”**

As Abraham found healing, he was also equipped to help others. What began as personal restoration became a source of renewed strength for his wider community.

![Image 7](https://www.silglobal.site/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/blog_post_header_950_x_502_px_8.png)

[More Stories](https://global.sil.org/stories-news/?_filter=community-wellbeing)

## What We Do

###### Trauma healing

We develop Bible-based trauma healing materials, facilitate group sessions, and train local facilitators to guide individuals and communities toward healing and restoration.

###### Faith & Farming

We create locally relevant teaching resources that connect biblical principles with sustainable agriculture, helping communities care for creation and strengthen food security.

###### Health Communication

We work with local partners to translate and adapt life-saving health and civic information into local languages, enabling informed decisions and collective action.

###### Community Strengthening

We equip families, churches, and local leaders with tools to nurture healthy relationships, prevent violence, and foster reconciliation and belonging.

###### Language revitalization

We collaborate with communities to restore and strengthen languages at risk of disappearing, supporting intergenerational transmission through literacy, storytelling, and cultural celebration.

###### Language Use Planning

We help communities identify how their languages can be used across sectors — education, health, business, and governance — to support inclusion and participation in all areas of life.

**“I had never allowed myself to cry before,” he said. “But there, I felt safe. I shared my grief, and I wept. We wept together. And I truly understood that I am not alone. That moment of release — that is when my own healing began.”**

As Abraham found healing, he was also equipped to help others. What began as personal restoration became a source of renewed strength for his wider community.

![Image 7](https://www.silglobal.site/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/blog_post_header_950_x_502_px_8.png)

[More Stories](https://global.sil.org/stories-news/?_filter=community-wellbeing)

## What We Do

###### Trauma healing

We develop Bible-based trauma healing materials, facilitate group sessions, and train local facilitators to guide individuals and communities toward healing and restoration.

###### Faith & Farming

We create locally relevant teaching resources that connect biblical principles with sustainable agriculture, helping communities care for creation and strengthen food security.

###### Health Communication

We work with local partners to translate and adapt life-saving health and civic information into local languages, enabling informed decisions and collective action.

###### Community Strengthening

We equip families, churches, and local leaders with tools to nurture healthy relationships, prevent violence, and foster reconciliation and belonging.

###### Language revitalization

We collaborate with communities to restore and strengthen languages at risk of disappearing, supporting intergenerational transmission through literacy, storytelling, and cultural celebration.

###### Language Use Planning

We help communities identify how their languages can be used across sectors — education, health, business, and governance — to support inclusion and participation in all areas of life.

# Learning

![Image 6](https://www.silglobal.site/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2015Aug_Bangladesh_362.jpg)

#### Nearly 40% of children and adults worldwide cannot access education in a language they understand.

Minority language speakers are often forced to use other languages in school and economic activity, leading to frustration, confusion, and missed opportunities. When education begins in a language people don’t yet understand, many are left behind.

## Our Approach

We walk alongside communities to remove the language-related barriers that stand in the way of learning. Together, we develop writing systems, literacy tools, and educational materials in the languages people know best, the ones they first spoke at home.

From early-grade classrooms to adult learning programs, our goal is to help communities build a strong foundation for learning that lasts a lifetime. By combining linguistic research, literacy methods, and digital innovation, we help communities design solutions that fit their culture and context, empowering children, youth, and adults to learn with confidence and dignity.

**When people learn in their own language, it leads to lifelong impact:**

*    Children grasp lessons faster and build a solid foundation for future learning. 
*    Adults gain literacy skills that open doors to jobs, leadership, and civic participation. 
*    Families can read and understand information that affects their wellbeing. 
*    Communities preserve and strengthen their languages for the next generation. 

## Featured Story

###### “I Have Become A Child Again!”

Despite lined face and steady gaze, René Epeiyu feels like a child again. What can reinvigorate a man’s mind in such a way? The simple answer—learning. ###### EDUCATIONAL MATERIALS

#### Nearly 40% of children and adults worldwide cannot access education in a language they understand.

Minority language speakers are often forced to use other languages in school and economic activity, leading to frustration, confusion, and missed opportunities. When education begins in a language people don’t yet understand, many are left behind.

## Our Approach

We walk alongside communities to remove the language-related barriers that stand in the way of learning. Together, we develop writing systems, literacy tools, and educational materials in the languages people know best, the ones they first spoke at home.

From early-grade classrooms to adult learning programs, our goal is to help communities build a strong foundation for learning that lasts a lifetime. By combining linguistic research, literacy methods, and digital innovation, we help communities design solutions that fit their culture and context, empowering children, youth, and adults to learn with confidence and dignity.

**When people learn in their own language, it leads to lifelong impact:**

*    Children grasp lessons faster and build a solid foundation for future learning. 
*    Adults gain literacy skills that open doors to jobs, leadership, and civic participation. 
*    Families can read and understand information that affects their wellbeing. 
*    Communities preserve and strengthen their languages for the next generation.

**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an [evangelical Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelicalism "Evangelicalism") nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document [languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language "Language"), especially those that are lesser-known, to expand [linguistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistics "Linguistics") knowledge, promote [literacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy "Literacy"), translate the Christian [Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible "Bible") into local languages, and aid [minority language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_language "Minority language") development.

Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _[Ethnologue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnologue "Ethnologue")_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)

Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas"), Texas.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Early history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early history")]

[William Cameron Townsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Cameron_Townsend "William Cameron Townsend"), a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a [Christian mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_mission "Christian mission") with the [Disciples of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Church_(Disciples_of_Christ) "Christian Church (Disciples of Christ)") among the [Kaqchikel Maya people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaqchikel_people "Kaqchikel people") in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican [Secretariat of Public Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretariat_of_Public_Education_(Mexico) "Secretariat of Public Education (Mexico)") under the government of President [Lázaro Cárdenas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1zaro_C%C3%A1rdenas "Lázaro Cárdenas") (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-[missionaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missionary "Missionary") to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded [Wycliffe Bible Translators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wycliffe_Bible_Translators "Wycliffe Bible Translators") in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)

Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in [Sulphur Springs, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulphur_Springs,_Benton_County,_Arkansas "Sulphur Springs, Benton County, Arkansas"), in 1934 to train missionaries in basic [linguistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistics "Linguistics"), [anthropological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropology "Anthropology"), and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, [Kenneth Lee Pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Lee_Pike "Kenneth Lee Pike") (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia")]

Main article: [Chet Bitterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Bitterman "Chet Bitterman")

On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by [far-left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far-left "Far-left") guerilla group [M-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_of_April_Movement "19th of April Movement") in Colombia who believed SIL was a [cover operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covert_operation "Covert operation") for the [Central Intelligence Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency") (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)

M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)

### 2000–present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2000–present")]

In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)

In 2023[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit), SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)

## Vision and mission

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Vision and mission")]

The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)

## Contributions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Contributions")]

SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as [Hixkaryana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hixkaryana_language "Hixkaryana language") and [Pirahã](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirah%C3%A3_language "Pirahã language"), which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)

SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but [tagmemics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagmemics "Tagmemics"), though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by [Kenneth Pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Pike "Kenneth Pike"), who also coined the words [emic and etic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emic_and_etic "Emic and etic"), more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)

Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)

SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), these include [Dallas International University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_International_University "Dallas International University"), [Biola University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biola_University "Biola University"), [Moody Bible Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Bible_Institute "Moody Bible Institute"), and [Dallas Theological Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Theological_Seminary "Dallas Theological Seminary"). Other universities with SIL programs include [Trinity Western University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Western_University "Trinity Western University") in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Charles Darwin University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin_University "Charles Darwin University") in [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), and [Universidad Ricardo Palma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_Ricardo_Palma "Universidad Ricardo Palma") in Lima, Peru.

The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)
