## Methodological contributions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Methodological contributions")]

### Ethnologue and ISO 639-3 codes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Ethnologue and ISO 639-3 codes")]

Main article: [Ethnologue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnologue "Ethnologue")

_Ethnologue: A Guide to the World's Languages_ has been published by SIL since 1951.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-22)

From the 13th edition (1997) onwards, the entire contents of the published book were also shared online. From the 17th edition onwards (2013) the publication shifted to a web-centric paradigm, meaning that the website is now the primary means by which the database is accessed. Among other advantages, this greatly facilitates user contributions. A new edition is now published every February. The 29th edition was released in February 2026 and lists 7,170 languages.

Starting with the 16th edition (2009), _Ethnologue_ uses the [ISO 639-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_639-3 "ISO 639-3") standard, which assigns 3-letter codes to languages; these were derived in part from the 3-letter codes that were used in the _Ethnologue_'s 15th edition. SIL is the [registration authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registration_authority "Registration authority") for the ISO 639-3 standard.

With the publication of the 17th edition (2016), Ethnologue launched a subscription service, claiming that the paywall would only affect 5% of users.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-23) Users who contribute over 100 accepted changes are rewarded with lifetime free access.

A comprehensive review of the 16th, 17th and 18th editions acknowledged that "[Ethnologue] is at present still better than any other non-derivative work of the same scope" except that "[it] fails to disclose the sources for the information presented.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-24)

### Software

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Software")]

SIL has developed widely used software for linguistic research.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-25)

*   Adapt It is a tool for translating text from one language into a related language after performing limited linguistic analysis.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-26)
*   In the field of [lexicon collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_lexicology "Computational lexicology"), ShoeBox, the newer ToolBox (Field Linguist's Toolbox),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-27) and Lexique Pro[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-28) have largely been replaced by FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx Windows and Linux)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-31) for linguists and WeSay (also Windows and Linux)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-34) for non-professionals. SIL also provides a "Webonary" website for publishing dictionaries.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-35)
*   [Graphite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite_(SIL) "Graphite (SIL)") is a smart-font technology and rendering system.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-38)
*   Keyman is a keyboard software solution for typing over 2000 of the world's languages and can be used to make custom keyboards.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-41)

### Fonts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Fonts")]

SIL has developed several widely used font sets that it makes available as [free software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_software "Free software") under the [SIL Open Font License](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Open_Font_License "SIL Open Font License") (OFL).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-42) The names of SIL fonts reflect the Biblical mission of the organization _charis_ (Greek for "grace"), _doulos_ (Greek for "servant") and _gentium_ (Latin for "of the nations"). These fonts have become standard resources for linguists working on the documentation of the world's languages.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDobrinGood2009-43) Most of them are designed only for specific writing systems, such as [Ethiopic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Semitic_languages "Ethiopian Semitic languages"), [Devanagari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devanagari "Devanagari"), [New Tai Lue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Tai_Lue_alphabet "New Tai Lue alphabet"), [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_alphabet "Hebrew alphabet"), [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_alphabet "Arabic alphabet"), [Khmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_alphabet "Khmer alphabet"), [Yi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yi_script "Yi script"), [Myanmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar_script "Myanmar script"), [Coptic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coptic_alphabet "Coptic alphabet"), and [Tai Viet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tai_Viet_script "Tai Viet script"), or some more technical notation, such as [cipher musical notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_musical_notation "Numbered musical notation") or [IPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Phonetic_Alphabet "International Phonetic Alphabet"). Fonts that support Latin include:

*   [Gentium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentium "Gentium"): "a typeface family designed to enable the diverse ethnic groups around the world who use the Latin, Cyrillic and Greek scripts to produce readable, high-quality publications. It supports a wide range of Latin- and Cyrillic-based alphabets."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-44)
*   [Doulos SIL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doulos_SIL "Doulos SIL"): "a Unicode serif font similar in design to [Times/Times New Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_New_Roman "Times New Roman"). It contains a comprehensive inventory of glyphs needed for almost any Roman- or Cyrillic-based writing system, whether used for phonetic or orthographic needs. In addition, there is provision for other characters and symbols useful to linguists. It contains near-complete coverage of all the characters defined in Unicode 7.0 for Latin and Cyrillic."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-47)
*   [Charis SIL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charis_SIL "Charis SIL"): "a Unicode-based font family that supports the wide range of languages that use the Latin and Cyrillic scripts. It is specially designed to make long texts pleasant and easy to read, even in less than ideal reproduction and display environments."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-50)
*   [Andika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andika_(font) "Andika (font)"): "a sans serif Unicode font designed especially for literacy use and the needs of beginning readers. The focus is on clear letterforms that will not be easily confused with one another. It supports near-complete coverage for Latin and Cyrillic."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-51)

## Recognitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Recognitions")]

The 1947 Summer Meeting of the [Linguistic Society of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistic_Society_of_America "Linguistic Society of America") passed a resolution that the work of SIL "should be strongly commended by our Society and welcomed as one of the most promising developments in applied linguistics in this country."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-52)

SIL holds formal consultative status with [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") and the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") and has been publicly recognized by UNESCO for their work in many parts of Asia.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-53) SIL also holds [non-governmental organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organization "Non-governmental organization") status in many countries.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

SIL's work has received appreciation and recognition in several international settings. In 1973, SIL was awarded the [Ramon Magsaysay Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay_Award "Ramon Magsaysay Award") for International Understanding. This foundation honors outstanding individuals and organizations working in Asia who manifest greatness of spirit in service to the peoples of Asia.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-54) UNESCO Literacy Prizes have been awarded to SIL's work in a number of countries: Australia (1969), Cameroon (1986), Papua New Guinea (1979), Philippines (1991).[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-55)

## Criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Criticism")]

In 1979, SIL's agreement was officially terminated by the Mexican government after critiques from anthropologists regarding the combination of education and missionary activities in indigenous communities, though SIL continued to be active in that country.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2001182-56) At a conference of the Inter-American Indian Institute in [Mérida, Yucatán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9rida,_Yucat%C3%A1n "Mérida, Yucatán"), in November 1980, delegates denounced the Summer Institute of Linguistics, charging that it was using a scientific name to conceal its [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant "Protestant") agenda and an alleged [capitalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism "Capitalism") view that was alien to indigenous traditions.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonner199920-57)

SIL was also expelled from [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador "Ecuador"), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico"), and [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama"), and restricted in [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia") and [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClearySteigenga200436-58) It currently operates in Brazil, Mexico, and Peru.

Some linguists and anthropologists have criticized SIL's focus on language description, language development, Bible translation, and missionary activities as an effort to change indigenous cultures, which exacerbates the problems that cause [language endangerment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered_language "Endangered language") and [language death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_death "Language death").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHvalkofAaby1981-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErrington2008153%E2%80%93162-61) Linguists have argued that the missionary focus of SIL makes relations with academic linguists and their reliance on SIL software and knowledge infrastructure problematic in that respective goals, while often overlapping, also sometimes diverge considerably.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDobrin2009-62)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDobrinGood2009-43)

SIL does not consider efforts to change cultural patterns a form of cultural destruction and points out that all their work is based on the voluntary participation of indigenous peoples. In the SIL view, [ethnocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnocide "Ethnocide") is not a valid concept and it would lead to pessimism to characterize culture change resulting from the inevitable progress of civilization as ethnocide.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOlson2009-63)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDobrin2009-62) SIL sees itself as actively protecting endangered languages by promoting them within the speech community and providing mother-tongue literacy training.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-64)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDobrin2009-62) Additionally, their expanded interest in preserving threatened languages has resulted in the creation of a Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

### Accusations of ethnocide against the Waorani

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Accusations of ethnocide against the Waorani")]

SIL has been accused of ethnocide against the Waorani people in Ecuador and of colluding with oil companies to dispossess the Waorani people of their territory for oil exploration and exploitation. "The violent process of [forced displacement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_displacement "Forced displacement"), [acculturation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acculturation "Acculturation"), ethnocide, and the spread of diseases, imposed by SIL under the shadow of oil interests, is possibly one of the most profound and dramatic changes that the [Waorani people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waorani_people "Waorani people") have experienced in their history."[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-65)

SIL missionaries first arrived in [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador "Ecuador") in 1952 with the objective of evangelizing the Waorani [indigenous people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples "Indigenous peoples") of the [Ecuadorian Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriente_(Ecuador) "Oriente (Ecuador)"), who had remained in [voluntary isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncontacted_peoples "Uncontacted peoples") until then.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-66) In 1955, they launched [Operation Auca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Auca "Operation Auca") to force contact with the Waorani, with the support of oil companies willing to expand exploration,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-67) most notably [Royal Dutch Shell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_plc "Shell plc") and [Texaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texaco "Texaco"). On January 6, 1956, a group of Waorani killed five US missionaries of Operation Auca in Playa Palma within Waorani territory, where they had landed and established a temporary base. In 1957, [Rachel Saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Saint "Rachel Saint"), whose brother ([Nate Saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nate_Saint "Nate Saint")) was killed in the January 1956 attack, embarked on a tour of the United States together with [Dayuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dayuma "Dayuma"), one of the first contacted Waorani persons, appearing with [Billy Graham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Graham "Billy Graham") at [Madison Square Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Square_Garden "Madison Square Garden") and on [Ralph Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Edwards "Ralph Edwards")' television show _[This Is Your Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Is\_Your\_Life\_(American\_franchise) "This Is Your Life (American franchise)")_, thus turning the conversion of the Waoranis into a [cause célèbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cause_c%C3%A9l%C3%A8bre "Cause célèbre") in the United States, increasing donations and support for evangelism efforts in Ecuador.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-68)

Subsequently, presence and activity of SIL grew in Ecuador and, in 1968, SIL signed a formal agreement with the [Ecuadorian Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuadorian_government "Ecuadorian government") to "pacify the savages" and establishing a 1,600 km 2 (620 sq mi) "protectorate" in [Limoncocha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoncocha_National_Biological_Reserve "Limoncocha National Biological Reserve") and Tiweno, covering the western part of Waorani territory.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:6-69) It aimed at concentrating and evangelizing the Waorani population, which "triggered profound changes: forced displacement, loss of territory, and a significant decline in their population due to disease."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:6-69) By 1972, most Waorani had been concentrated in Tiweno to be converted, with the groups from the lower [Cononaco river](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cononaco_River "Cononaco River"), who lived near the [Yasuní](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasun%C3%AD_River "Yasuní River") and Nashiño rivers (nampaweiris, waneiris, baiwairis, kempereiris) remaining.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70)

The Waorani population before the 1950s contact was estimated at at least 600 persons, but contact with the SIL missionaries, oil workers, loggers and other indigenous peoples introduced diseases like influenza, tuberculosis, malaria, and polio, which were deadly for the until then isolated Waorani.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70) Waorani accounts indicate that those remaining in their territory believed it was the SIL missionaries who "poisoned the [chicha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicha "Chicha")" and that "God is bad because he let [them] die".[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70) In 1969, "a deadly polio epidemic hit the missionary compound [...] immediately following the arrival of the third Waorani group, killing 16 and permanently handicapping many more; several authors argue that SIL was directly responsible for this outbreak due to inadequate vaccinations and sanitation while at the same time concentrating a large population in such a small area."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:7-71) Records indicate that approximately 525 Waoranis were concentrated in the SIL "protectorate", over 80% of their pre-contact population, "confined to a small area, living sedentary, missionary dependent lives."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:7-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:2-72)

Resistance to evangelism by SIL missionaries before 1968 and then to concentration in the "protectorate" was constant, with violent conflict erupting between different groups of the Waorani, attacks against oil workers and against persons of other indigenous peoples living in the area.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-73) In 1968, the Waorani leader Tagae and other families separated refused to be displaced to the missionary settlement, and have since lived in voluntary isolation. Today, they are referred to as the [Tagaeri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagaeri "Tagaeri"), an indigenous group living in voluntary isolation. In 1972 "Waorani leaders like Wiñame and Dabo rebelled and founded new settlements in places like Dayuno."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:6-69)

Facing a decrease in population in the "protectorate" due to death of flight, in 1976, the SIL missionaries called the missionary anthropologist James Yost to "explain the reasons for the failed [reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductions "Reductions"). Yost recommended dispersing the groups (some clans had already become enemies and left the reserve). He also suggested SIL's withdrawal from Tiweno 'so that the Waorani can decide their own destiny'",[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70) admitting in 1978 that "if the Waorani were to solve their own problems and remain independent of SIL, they would need to face their problems alone."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-74) SIL would then progressively reduce its presence in the "protectorate".

However, the Ecuadorian Government had declared the Waorani territory as vacant and started leasing it to oil companies,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-75) in particular Texaco, and handed property right to "colonizers"[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:2-72) under the 1977 Law on Colonization of the Amazon Region, causing further conflicts. Faced with dispossession, many Waorani men turned to working for the oil companies or leaving their territory entirely. "By the end of 1979, James Yost counted more than seventy men [in the "protectorate"] (sixty percent of the total) who had worked for oil companies at least once, compared with thirty-three a year earlier and fewer than ten before 1977. Thirteen single girls were working as domestic servants in cities."[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-76)

By the 1980s, SIL activities in Ecuador, not only in the Amazon, were a matter of national concern, with indigenous leaders calling for their expulsion from the country. In May 1981, [Blanca Chancoso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanca_Chancoso "Blanca Chancoso"), leader of the Confederación de Pueblos de la Nacionalidad Kichwa del Ecuador ([Ecuarunari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECUARUNARI "ECUARUNARI")) stated that "for a long time we have been denouncing these facts and the damage [SIL] have caused to our indigenous communities throughout the country",[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-77) and demanded they be expelled from Ecuador. The [left-wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics") president of Ecuador of the time [Jaime Roldós Aguilera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaime_Rold%C3%B3s_Aguilera "Jaime Roldós Aguilera") expelled SIL by Decree 1159 of May 22, 1981,[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:3-78) among mounting allegations of [espionage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espionage "Espionage") in favour of oil companies[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70) and of SIL's collaboration with the [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency") in Latin America.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-80) Reacting to the expulsion, in November 1981, local activists stated to the [International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Work_Group_for_Indigenous_Affairs "International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs") (IWGIA) that "from its inception in 1952, the Institute's activities have been linked to those of oil companies, which used SIL's policies to confine the indigenous peoples of the Amazon to a tenth of their original territory. Its educational work has had a profound impact on the way of life of the contacted groups, resulting in the disintegration of the indigenous worldview and a process of forced assimilation into mainstream society, which has led to the impoverishment of a large number of indigenous people. Recently, SIL has attempted to expand its reach to other groups living on the coast and in the highlands."[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:3-78)

In 1986, SIL unsuccessfully tried to renegotiate its entry into the country. Nevertheless, some SIL missionaries returned to Ecuador and their influence continued, specially that of Rachel Saint, who is said to have controlled access to Tiweno, allegedly barring anybody who was not a member of SIL, up until her death in 1994.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70)

SIL has also been accused of [biopiracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biopiracy "Biopiracy") of Waorani blood in collusion with the Ecuadorian Government and the oil company [Maxus](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxus%20Energy%20Corporation "fr:Maxus Energy Corporation").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:4-81) "In 2012, the Waorani nationality, known as Nacionalidad Waorani del Ecuador (NAWE), brought to the attention the use of genetic samples to the government, to which the natives state that the samples were taken from the community without their consent."[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Ortiz-Prado_2020-82) Reportedly, the collection of the samples took place mostly between 1990 and 1991. In 2014, René Ramírez, the head of the Ecuadorian Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Technology stated that "it was demonstrated that the [Coriell Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriell_Institute_for_Medical_Research "Coriell Institute for Medical Research") has in its stores samples (from the Waorani) and that it sells genetic material from the Waorani people."[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-83) He further explained that "[Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") was among the purchasers. Specifically, [a 2012 report] found that since 1994, seven cell cultures and 36 blood samples were distributed to eight different countries. However, scientific publications based on the samples have stated that the samples used for their own studies date back to the 1970s,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-84) when SIL was in charge of the "protectorate" and was conducting the vaccination campaigns. Allegedly, it was "during vaccinations initiated by the SIL in 1979 by Jonathan E. Kaplan, James W. Larrick, and James Yost, that the first blood samples were taken from Waorani people".[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:4-81)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-85) The presence of SIL translators during the collection of Waorani blood has been ratified by the alleged Waorani victims themselves.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Ortiz-Prado_2020-82)

**SIL Global** (formerly known as the **Summer Institute of Linguistics International**) is an [evangelical Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelicalism "Evangelicalism") nonprofit organization whose main purpose is to study, develop and document [languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language "Language"), especially those that are lesser-known, to expand [linguistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistics "Linguistics") knowledge, promote [literacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy "Literacy"), translate the Christian [Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible "Bible") into local languages, and aid [minority language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_language "Minority language") development.

Based on its language documentation work, SIL publishes a database, _[Ethnologue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnologue "Ethnologue")_, of its research into the world's languages, and develops and publishes software programs for language documentation, such as FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2) and Lexique Pro.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)

Its main offices in the United States are located at the International Linguistics Center in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas"), Texas.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Early history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early history")]

[William Cameron Townsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Cameron_Townsend "William Cameron Townsend"), a Presbyterian minister, founded the organization in 1934, after undertaking a [Christian mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_mission "Christian mission") with the [Disciples of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Church_(Disciples_of_Christ) "Christian Church (Disciples of Christ)") among the [Kaqchikel Maya people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaqchikel_people "Kaqchikel people") in Guatemala in the early 1930s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-5) In 1933, he turned to Mexico to translate the Bible into indigenous languages there, as he had done for Kaqchikel. Townsend established a working relationship with the Mexican [Secretariat of Public Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretariat_of_Public_Education_(Mexico) "Secretariat of Public Education (Mexico)") under the government of President [Lázaro Cárdenas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1zaro_C%C3%A1rdenas "Lázaro Cárdenas") (in office 1934–1940) and founded SIL to educate linguist-[missionaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missionary "Missionary") to work in Mexico. Because the Mexican government did not allow missionary work through its educational system, Townsend founded [Wycliffe Bible Translators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wycliffe_Bible_Translators "Wycliffe Bible Translators") in 1942 as a separate organization from SIL. Wycliffe Bible Translators focused on Bible translation and missionary activities, whereas SIL focused on linguistic documentation and literacy education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-6)

Having initiated collaboration with the Mexican education authorities, Townsend started the institute as a small summer training session in [Sulphur Springs, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulphur_Springs,_Benton_County,_Arkansas "Sulphur Springs, Benton County, Arkansas"), in 1934 to train missionaries in basic [linguistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistics "Linguistics"), [anthropological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropology "Anthropology"), and translation principles. Through the following decades, the SIL linguists worked at providing literacy education to indigenous people of Mexico, while simultaneously working with the Wycliffe Bible Translators on Bible translation. One of the students at the first summer institute in its second year, 1935, [Kenneth Lee Pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Lee_Pike "Kenneth Lee Pike") (1912–2000), would become the foremost figure in the history of SIL.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-G255-4) He served as SIL's president from 1942 to 1979, then as president emeritus until he died in 2000.

### Instituto Lingüístico de Verano

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano")]

The Mexican branch, _[Instituto Lingüístico de Verano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instituto\_Ling%C3%BC%C3%ADstico\_de\_Verano\_(Mexico) "Instituto Lingüístico de Verano (Mexico)")_, was established in 1948.

### Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Kidnapping and murder of Chester A. Bitterman in Colombia")]

Main article: [Chet Bitterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Bitterman "Chet Bitterman")

On January 19, 1981, SIL field worker Chester "Chet" A. Bitterman was taken hostage by [far-left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far-left "Far-left") guerilla group [M-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_of_April_Movement "19th of April Movement") in Colombia who believed SIL was a [cover operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covert_operation "Covert operation") for the [Central Intelligence Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency") (CIA). SIL denied involvement with any government intelligence agency stating that it was against their policy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-8)

M-19 demanded SIL withdraw all 209 of its people from Colombia, or else they would kill Bitterman. After 48 days of SIL refusing to yield to the demands, Bitterman was found murdered.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-9)

### 2000–present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2000–present")]

In 2016, Michel Kenmogne from Cameroon became executive director. In 2025, Johnstone Ndunde became executive director.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-10)

In 2023[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit), SIL said it had 1,350 language projects in 98 countries and 4,200 staff from 84 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) By 2023, this had risen to 1,530 language projects in 107 countries, with a corresponding increase in staff to 4,373 people from 86 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11) The organization reports that these languages are spoken by 950 million people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-12)

## Vision and mission

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Vision and mission")]

The vision of SIL Global is: "We long to see people flourishing in community using the languages they value most." Their mission states: "Inspired by God's love, we advocate, build capacity, and work with local communities to apply language expertise that advances meaningful development, education, and engagement with Scripture."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:0-11)

## Contributions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Contributions")]

SIL's principal contribution to linguistics has been the data that have been gathered and analyzed from over 1,000 minority and endangered languages,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-13) many of which had not been previously studied academically. SIL endeavors to share both its data and the results of its analysis to contribute to the overall knowledge of language. This has resulted in publications on languages such as [Hixkaryana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hixkaryana_language "Hixkaryana language") and [Pirahã](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirah%C3%A3_language "Pirahã language"), which have challenged the universality of some linguistic theories. SIL's work has resulted in over 20,000 technical publications, all of which are listed in the SIL Bibliography.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-14) Most of these are a reflection of linguistic fieldwork.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-15)

SIL's focus has not been on the development of new linguistic theories, but [tagmemics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagmemics "Tagmemics"), though no longer promoted by SIL, was developed by [Kenneth Pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Pike "Kenneth Pike"), who also coined the words [emic and etic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emic_and_etic "Emic and etic"), more widely used today in anthropology.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-16)

Another focus of SIL is literacy work, particularly in indigenous languages. SIL assists local, regional, and national agencies that are developing formal and informal education in vernacular languages. These cooperative efforts enable new advances in the complex field of educational development in multilingual and multicultural societies.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-17)

SIL provides instructors and instructional materials for linguistics programs at several major institutions of higher learning around the world. In the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), these include [Dallas International University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_International_University "Dallas International University"), [Biola University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biola_University "Biola University"), [Moody Bible Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Bible_Institute "Moody Bible Institute"), and [Dallas Theological Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Theological_Seminary "Dallas Theological Seminary"). Other universities with SIL programs include [Trinity Western University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Western_University "Trinity Western University") in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Charles Darwin University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin_University "Charles Darwin University") in [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), and [Universidad Ricardo Palma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_Ricardo_Palma "Universidad Ricardo Palma") in Lima, Peru.

The organization has recently established a new Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit that aims to preserve and revitalize languages threatened by extinction. The creation of this department reflects a growing interest in documenting endangered languages and incorporates a multidisciplinary approach to anthropology and linguistics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

## Methodological contributions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Methodological contributions")]

### Ethnologue and ISO 639-3 codes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Ethnologue and ISO 639-3 codes")]

Main article: [Ethnologue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnologue "Ethnologue")

_Ethnologue: A Guide to the World's Languages_ has been published by SIL since 1951.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-22)

From the 13th edition (1997) onwards, the entire contents of the published book were also shared online. From the 17th edition onwards (2013) the publication shifted to a web-centric paradigm, meaning that the website is now the primary means by which the database is accessed. Among other advantages, this greatly facilitates user contributions. A new edition is now published every February. The 29th edition was released in February 2026 and lists 7,170 languages.

Starting with the 16th edition (2009), _Ethnologue_ uses the [ISO 639-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_639-3 "ISO 639-3") standard, which assigns 3-letter codes to languages; these were derived in part from the 3-letter codes that were used in the _Ethnologue_'s 15th edition. SIL is the [registration authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registration_authority "Registration authority") for the ISO 639-3 standard.

With the publication of the 17th edition (2016), Ethnologue launched a subscription service, claiming that the paywall would only affect 5% of users.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-23) Users who contribute over 100 accepted changes are rewarded with lifetime free access.

A comprehensive review of the 16th, 17th and 18th editions acknowledged that "[Ethnologue] is at present still better than any other non-derivative work of the same scope" except that "[it] fails to disclose the sources for the information presented.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-24)

### Software

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Software")]

SIL has developed widely used software for linguistic research.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-25)

*   Adapt It is a tool for translating text from one language into a related language after performing limited linguistic analysis.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-26)
*   In the field of [lexicon collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_lexicology "Computational lexicology"), ShoeBox, the newer ToolBox (Field Linguist's Toolbox),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-27) and Lexique Pro[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Lexique_Pro-3)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-28) have largely been replaced by FieldWorks Language Explorer (FLEx Windows and Linux)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Fi-2)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-31) for linguists and WeSay (also Windows and Linux)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-34) for non-professionals. SIL also provides a "Webonary" website for publishing dictionaries.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-35)
*   [Graphite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite_(SIL) "Graphite (SIL)") is a smart-font technology and rendering system.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-38)
*   Keyman is a keyboard software solution for typing over 2000 of the world's languages and can be used to make custom keyboards.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-41)

### Fonts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Fonts")]

SIL has developed several widely used font sets that it makes available as [free software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_software "Free software") under the [SIL Open Font License](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Open_Font_License "SIL Open Font License") (OFL).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-42) The names of SIL fonts reflect the Biblical mission of the organization _charis_ (Greek for "grace"), _doulos_ (Greek for "servant") and _gentium_ (Latin for "of the nations"). These fonts have become standard resources for linguists working on the documentation of the world's languages.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDobrinGood2009-43) Most of them are designed only for specific writing systems, such as [Ethiopic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Semitic_languages "Ethiopian Semitic languages"), [Devanagari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devanagari "Devanagari"), [New Tai Lue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Tai_Lue_alphabet "New Tai Lue alphabet"), [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_alphabet "Hebrew alphabet"), [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_alphabet "Arabic alphabet"), [Khmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_alphabet "Khmer alphabet"), [Yi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yi_script "Yi script"), [Myanmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar_script "Myanmar script"), [Coptic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coptic_alphabet "Coptic alphabet"), and [Tai Viet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tai_Viet_script "Tai Viet script"), or some more technical notation, such as [cipher musical notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_musical_notation "Numbered musical notation") or [IPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Phonetic_Alphabet "International Phonetic Alphabet"). Fonts that support Latin include:

*   [Gentium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentium "Gentium"): "a typeface family designed to enable the diverse ethnic groups around the world who use the Latin, Cyrillic and Greek scripts to produce readable, high-quality publications. It supports a wide range of Latin- and Cyrillic-based alphabets."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-44)
*   [Doulos SIL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doulos_SIL "Doulos SIL"): "a Unicode serif font similar in design to [Times/Times New Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_New_Roman "Times New Roman"). It contains a comprehensive inventory of glyphs needed for almost any Roman- or Cyrillic-based writing system, whether used for phonetic or orthographic needs. In addition, there is provision for other characters and symbols useful to linguists. It contains near-complete coverage of all the characters defined in Unicode 7.0 for Latin and Cyrillic."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-47)
*   [Charis SIL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charis_SIL "Charis SIL"): "a Unicode-based font family that supports the wide range of languages that use the Latin and Cyrillic scripts. It is specially designed to make long texts pleasant and easy to read, even in less than ideal reproduction and display environments."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-50)
*   [Andika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andika_(font) "Andika (font)"): "a sans serif Unicode font designed especially for literacy use and the needs of beginning readers. The focus is on clear letterforms that will not be easily confused with one another. It supports near-complete coverage for Latin and Cyrillic."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-51)

## Recognitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Recognitions")]

The 1947 Summer Meeting of the [Linguistic Society of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistic_Society_of_America "Linguistic Society of America") passed a resolution that the work of SIL "should be strongly commended by our Society and welcomed as one of the most promising developments in applied linguistics in this country."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-52)

SIL holds formal consultative status with [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") and the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") and has been publicly recognized by UNESCO for their work in many parts of Asia.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-53) SIL also holds [non-governmental organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organization "Non-governmental organization") status in many countries.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

SIL's work has received appreciation and recognition in several international settings. In 1973, SIL was awarded the [Ramon Magsaysay Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay_Award "Ramon Magsaysay Award") for International Understanding. This foundation honors outstanding individuals and organizations working in Asia who manifest greatness of spirit in service to the peoples of Asia.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-54) UNESCO Literacy Prizes have been awarded to SIL's work in a number of countries: Australia (1969), Cameroon (1986), Papua New Guinea (1979), Philippines (1991).[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-55)

## Criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Criticism")]

In 1979, SIL's agreement was officially terminated by the Mexican government after critiques from anthropologists regarding the combination of education and missionary activities in indigenous communities, though SIL continued to be active in that country.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke2001182-56) At a conference of the Inter-American Indian Institute in [Mérida, Yucatán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9rida,_Yucat%C3%A1n "Mérida, Yucatán"), in November 1980, delegates denounced the Summer Institute of Linguistics, charging that it was using a scientific name to conceal its [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant "Protestant") agenda and an alleged [capitalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism "Capitalism") view that was alien to indigenous traditions.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonner199920-57)

SIL was also expelled from [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador "Ecuador"), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico"), and [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama"), and restricted in [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia") and [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClearySteigenga200436-58) It currently operates in Brazil, Mexico, and Peru.

Some linguists and anthropologists have criticized SIL's focus on language description, language development, Bible translation, and missionary activities as an effort to change indigenous cultures, which exacerbates the problems that cause [language endangerment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered_language "Endangered language") and [language death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_death "Language death").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHvalkofAaby1981-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErrington2008153%E2%80%93162-61) Linguists have argued that the missionary focus of SIL makes relations with academic linguists and their reliance on SIL software and knowledge infrastructure problematic in that respective goals, while often overlapping, also sometimes diverge considerably.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDobrin2009-62)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDobrinGood2009-43)

SIL does not consider efforts to change cultural patterns a form of cultural destruction and points out that all their work is based on the voluntary participation of indigenous peoples. In the SIL view, [ethnocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnocide "Ethnocide") is not a valid concept and it would lead to pessimism to characterize culture change resulting from the inevitable progress of civilization as ethnocide.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOlson2009-63)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDobrin2009-62) SIL sees itself as actively protecting endangered languages by promoting them within the speech community and providing mother-tongue literacy training.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-64)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDobrin2009-62) Additionally, their expanded interest in preserving threatened languages has resulted in the creation of a Language and Culture Documentation Services Unit.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-La-18)

### Accusations of ethnocide against the Waorani

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SIL_Global&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Accusations of ethnocide against the Waorani")]

SIL has been accused of ethnocide against the Waorani people in Ecuador and of colluding with oil companies to dispossess the Waorani people of their territory for oil exploration and exploitation. "The violent process of [forced displacement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_displacement "Forced displacement"), [acculturation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acculturation "Acculturation"), ethnocide, and the spread of diseases, imposed by SIL under the shadow of oil interests, is possibly one of the most profound and dramatic changes that the [Waorani people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waorani_people "Waorani people") have experienced in their history."[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-65)

SIL missionaries first arrived in [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador "Ecuador") in 1952 with the objective of evangelizing the Waorani [indigenous people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples "Indigenous peoples") of the [Ecuadorian Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriente_(Ecuador) "Oriente (Ecuador)"), who had remained in [voluntary isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncontacted_peoples "Uncontacted peoples") until then.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-66) In 1955, they launched [Operation Auca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Auca "Operation Auca") to force contact with the Waorani, with the support of oil companies willing to expand exploration,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-67) most notably [Royal Dutch Shell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_plc "Shell plc") and [Texaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texaco "Texaco"). On January 6, 1956, a group of Waorani killed five US missionaries of Operation Auca in Playa Palma within Waorani territory, where they had landed and established a temporary base. In 1957, [Rachel Saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Saint "Rachel Saint"), whose brother ([Nate Saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nate_Saint "Nate Saint")) was killed in the January 1956 attack, embarked on a tour of the United States together with [Dayuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dayuma "Dayuma"), one of the first contacted Waorani persons, appearing with [Billy Graham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Graham "Billy Graham") at [Madison Square Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Square_Garden "Madison Square Garden") and on [Ralph Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Edwards "Ralph Edwards")' television show _[This Is Your Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Is\_Your\_Life\_(American\_franchise) "This Is Your Life (American franchise)")_, thus turning the conversion of the Waoranis into a [cause célèbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cause_c%C3%A9l%C3%A8bre "Cause célèbre") in the United States, increasing donations and support for evangelism efforts in Ecuador.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-68)

Subsequently, presence and activity of SIL grew in Ecuador and, in 1968, SIL signed a formal agreement with the [Ecuadorian Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuadorian_government "Ecuadorian government") to "pacify the savages" and establishing a 1,600 km 2 (620 sq mi) "protectorate" in [Limoncocha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoncocha_National_Biological_Reserve "Limoncocha National Biological Reserve") and Tiweno, covering the western part of Waorani territory.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:6-69) It aimed at concentrating and evangelizing the Waorani population, which "triggered profound changes: forced displacement, loss of territory, and a significant decline in their population due to disease."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:6-69) By 1972, most Waorani had been concentrated in Tiweno to be converted, with the groups from the lower [Cononaco river](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cononaco_River "Cononaco River"), who lived near the [Yasuní](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasun%C3%AD_River "Yasuní River") and Nashiño rivers (nampaweiris, waneiris, baiwairis, kempereiris) remaining.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70)

The Waorani population before the 1950s contact was estimated at at least 600 persons, but contact with the SIL missionaries, oil workers, loggers and other indigenous peoples introduced diseases like influenza, tuberculosis, malaria, and polio, which were deadly for the until then isolated Waorani.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70) Waorani accounts indicate that those remaining in their territory believed it was the SIL missionaries who "poisoned the [chicha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicha "Chicha")" and that "God is bad because he let [them] die".[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70) In 1969, "a deadly polio epidemic hit the missionary compound [...] immediately following the arrival of the third Waorani group, killing 16 and permanently handicapping many more; several authors argue that SIL was directly responsible for this outbreak due to inadequate vaccinations and sanitation while at the same time concentrating a large population in such a small area."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:7-71) Records indicate that approximately 525 Waoranis were concentrated in the SIL "protectorate", over 80% of their pre-contact population, "confined to a small area, living sedentary, missionary dependent lives."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:7-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:2-72)

Resistance to evangelism by SIL missionaries before 1968 and then to concentration in the "protectorate" was constant, with violent conflict erupting between different groups of the Waorani, attacks against oil workers and against persons of other indigenous peoples living in the area.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-73) In 1968, the Waorani leader Tagae and other families separated refused to be displaced to the missionary settlement, and have since lived in voluntary isolation. Today, they are referred to as the [Tagaeri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagaeri "Tagaeri"), an indigenous group living in voluntary isolation. In 1972 "Waorani leaders like Wiñame and Dabo rebelled and founded new settlements in places like Dayuno."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:6-69)

Facing a decrease in population in the "protectorate" due to death of flight, in 1976, the SIL missionaries called the missionary anthropologist James Yost to "explain the reasons for the failed [reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductions "Reductions"). Yost recommended dispersing the groups (some clans had already become enemies and left the reserve). He also suggested SIL's withdrawal from Tiweno 'so that the Waorani can decide their own destiny'",[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70) admitting in 1978 that "if the Waorani were to solve their own problems and remain independent of SIL, they would need to face their problems alone."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-74) SIL would then progressively reduce its presence in the "protectorate".

However, the Ecuadorian Government had declared the Waorani territory as vacant and started leasing it to oil companies,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-75) in particular Texaco, and handed property right to "colonizers"[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:2-72) under the 1977 Law on Colonization of the Amazon Region, causing further conflicts. Faced with dispossession, many Waorani men turned to working for the oil companies or leaving their territory entirely. "By the end of 1979, James Yost counted more than seventy men [in the "protectorate"] (sixty percent of the total) who had worked for oil companies at least once, compared with thirty-three a year earlier and fewer than ten before 1977. Thirteen single girls were working as domestic servants in cities."[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-76)

By the 1980s, SIL activities in Ecuador, not only in the Amazon, were a matter of national concern, with indigenous leaders calling for their expulsion from the country. In May 1981, [Blanca Chancoso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanca_Chancoso "Blanca Chancoso"), leader of the Confederación de Pueblos de la Nacionalidad Kichwa del Ecuador ([Ecuarunari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECUARUNARI "ECUARUNARI")) stated that "for a long time we have been denouncing these facts and the damage [SIL] have caused to our indigenous communities throughout the country",[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-77) and demanded they be expelled from Ecuador. The [left-wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics") president of Ecuador of the time [Jaime Roldós Aguilera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaime_Rold%C3%B3s_Aguilera "Jaime Roldós Aguilera") expelled SIL by Decree 1159 of May 22, 1981,[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:3-78) among mounting allegations of [espionage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espionage "Espionage") in favour of oil companies[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70) and of SIL's collaboration with the [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency") in Latin America.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-80) Reacting to the expulsion, in November 1981, local activists stated to the [International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Work_Group_for_Indigenous_Affairs "International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs") (IWGIA) that "from its inception in 1952, the Institute's activities have been linked to those of oil companies, which used SIL's policies to confine the indigenous peoples of the Amazon to a tenth of their original territory. Its educational work has had a profound impact on the way of life of the contacted groups, resulting in the disintegration of the indigenous worldview and a process of forced assimilation into mainstream society, which has led to the impoverishment of a large number of indigenous people. Recently, SIL has attempted to expand its reach to other groups living on the coast and in the highlands."[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:3-78)

In 1986, SIL unsuccessfully tried to renegotiate its entry into the country. Nevertheless, some SIL missionaries returned to Ecuador and their influence continued, specially that of Rachel Saint, who is said to have controlled access to Tiweno, allegedly barring anybody who was not a member of SIL, up until her death in 1994.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Andrade_2025-70)

SIL has also been accused of [biopiracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biopiracy "Biopiracy") of Waorani blood in collusion with the Ecuadorian Government and the oil company [Maxus](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxus%20Energy%20Corporation "fr:Maxus Energy Corporation").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:4-81) "In 2012, the Waorani nationality, known as Nacionalidad Waorani del Ecuador (NAWE), brought to the attention the use of genetic samples to the government, to which the natives state that the samples were taken from the community without their consent."[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Ortiz-Prado_2020-82) Reportedly, the collection of the samples took place mostly between 1990 and 1991. In 2014, René Ramírez, the head of the Ecuadorian Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Technology stated that "it was demonstrated that the [Coriell Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriell_Institute_for_Medical_Research "Coriell Institute for Medical Research") has in its stores samples (from the Waorani) and that it sells genetic material from the Waorani people."[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-83) He further explained that "[Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") was among the purchasers. Specifically, [a 2012 report] found that since 1994, seven cell cultures and 36 blood samples were distributed to eight different countries. However, scientific publications based on the samples have stated that the samples used for their own studies date back to the 1970s,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-84) when SIL was in charge of the "protectorate" and was conducting the vaccination campaigns. Allegedly, it was "during vaccinations initiated by the SIL in 1979 by Jonathan E. Kaplan, James W. Larrick, and James Yost, that the first blood samples were taken from Waorani people".[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-:4-81)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-85) The presence of SIL translators during the collection of Waorani blood has been ratified by the alleged Waorani victims themselves.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_Global#cite_note-Ortiz-Prado_2020-82)
